title: Test Your Understanding: Lifting State vs Context vs Global State
description: See how well you understood when to use lifted state, Context, and global stores!

questions.question: What is the recommended order of approaches when sharing state between components?

options.text: Context → Lifted state → Global store → Local state
Local state → Lifted state → Context → Global store
Global store → Context → Lifted state → Local state
Lifted state → Context → Local state → Global store

questions.explanation: Start with the simplest option that works. Local state first (if only one component needs it), then lift to a parent when 2–3 components share it, then Context when prop drilling hurts, and finally a global store when state is cross-cutting or updates frequently.

questions.question: When should you consider Context over lifted state?

options.text: When 2 sibling components need the same data
When you're passing the same prop through 3+ levels of components that don't use it
When state updates 60 times per second
When you need to persist state to localStorage

questions.explanation: Context is for when prop drilling becomes painful—passing props through components that don't use them. For 2 siblings, lifted state to their parent is enough. For high-frequency updates, Context causes re-render issues. For persistence, a store or useEffect is better.

questions.question: What is the main downside of using Context for frequently-updating state?

options.text: Context has a 1KB size limit
Every component that consumes the context re-renders when the value changes
Context cannot hold objects
Context only works in class components

questions.explanation: When the context value changes, every component that calls useContext for that context re-renders. For high-frequency updates (e.g., mouse position, form state), this causes performance problems. Use a store with selective subscriptions instead.

questions.question: Which scenario is best suited for a global store (Zustand, Redux)?

options.text: Theme (light/dark) used by 20 components
Shopping cart used in navbar, sidebar, checkout, and cart page
Tab selection shared by TabList and TabPanel
A modal's open/closed state

questions.explanation: A shopping cart is used across many unrelated parts of the app and may update frequently. A global store with selective subscriptions avoids re-rendering the whole app. Theme is better in Context (changes rarely). Tab selection and modal state are fine with lifted state.

questions.question: Splitting one large Context into multiple smaller contexts (e.g., ThemeContext, UserContext) can reduce unnecessary re-renders.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. When you have one context with user, theme, and sidebar state, any change re-renders all consumers. By splitting into ThemeContext, UserContext, and SidebarContext, a theme change only re-renders theme consumers—not user or sidebar consumers.

questions.question: Which of the following are good candidates for lifted state (props from parent)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tab selection shared by TabList and TabPanel
Theme used by 30 components across the app
Filter value shared by FilterBar and FilterResults (siblings)
Shopping cart used in 5 different pages
Modal open state shared by trigger button and modal

questions.explanation: Lifted state works when 2–3 nearby components need the data and the tree is shallow. Tabs, filter bar/results, and modal/button fit. Theme (30 components) and shopping cart (cross-cutting) need Context or a store.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of global stores like Zustand over Context for frequently-updating state?

options.text: Stores use less memory
Components can subscribe to specific slices of state and only re-render when those slices change
Stores work without a provider
Stores are built into React

questions.explanation: Zustand and similar stores support selective subscription: useCartStore((state) => state.items) means the component only re-renders when items changes, not when other store fields change. Context re-renders all consumers on any value change.

questions.question: You should default to using Redux or Zustand for all shared state 'for scalability.'

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Start with the simplest option. Most shared state can stay in lifted state or Context. Add a global store only when you have a concrete need: cross-cutting state, frequent updates with selective re-renders, persistence, or complex logic. Over-engineering early adds indirection and boilerplate.

questions.question: You have a filter dropdown with 200 options. Selecting a filter causes the whole filter panel to feel sluggish. The selected filter is in Context. What's the best fix?

options.text: Keep using Context but memoize the dropdown options
Move the filter state to lifted state or a store with selective subscription
Use React.memo on every component in the filter subtree
Reduce the number of options to 50

questions.explanation: The problem is that Context causes the entire consumer subtree to re-render on every selection. With 200 options, that's expensive. Moving to lifted state (if the filter is local to the panel) or a store with selective subscription (if shared) ensures only the components that need the filter value re-render.

questions.question: When lifting state, where should it live?

options.text: Always in the root App component
In the nearest common ancestor of the components that need it
In the first component that uses it
In a dedicated state container component

questions.explanation: Lift state to the nearest common ancestor of the components that need it—not higher. If ComponentA and ComponentB share a parent Panel, the state lives in Panel. Lifting to App adds unnecessary prop drilling through components that don't care about the state.
